I am fifty-six, and I have worked this land for thirty-five years. I never went to school, but the fields have been my teacher. This spring, with only three mouths in the house and some of us working off-farm, I must be careful with my labor. I have fourteen mu and a well for irrigation, so water is there, but electricity for the pump costs money, so I cannot waste it.

Here is how I will divide the land. Wheat and maize are my backbone—they feed us and give a steady income, and I can manage much of it by machine. I will put ten mu into the wheat-maize rotation. The wheat is already in the ground from last autumn; now I must tend it through to the June harvest, then plant maize immediately after. For the remaining four mu, I will plant two mu of chili and two mu of cotton. Chili brings good cash, and two mu is enough that I can pick and sell it without hiring too much help. Cotton is familiar to me, but it is heavy work, so I will not plant more than two mu.

For the wheat, I will use an improved variety like Jimai 22. I will rotary-till before the green-up, give it three irrigations from the well—green-up, jointing, and grain-filling—and apply about twenty-five kilograms of nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphate and a little potash. I expect around one thousand jin per mu, which is about one thousand kilograms.

When the wheat comes off in June, I will plant hybrid maize, Denghai 605, directly into the stubble with no-tillage. Maize grows fast in the summer heat. I will irrigate it twice and use less fertilizer than the wheat, around eighteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu. I expect roughly eleven hundred kilograms per mu.

For the cotton, I will rotary-till in spring and plant an improved variety. Cotton needs water at flowering and boll-setting, so three irrigations. It also attracts many pests, so I must spray often—about twelve times through the season. I will apply a balanced fertilizer and hope for about five hundred fifty kilograms of seed cotton per mu.

The chili will be rotary-tilled and planted in spring. Chili is thirsty and prone to disease, so I will irrigate four times and spray about eighteen times. It needs plenty of potash for the fruit, so I will give it more potassium than the grains. If the weather is kind, I should get around five thousand five hundred kilograms per mu of fresh chili.
